item.title: The role of upper–deep ocean heat exchange in shaping warming patterns and climate feedbacks in CMIP6 models
item.dc:creator: Guo Duan, Duoying Ji, Min Cui, 吕欣宇, Jiaxu Wang, Yongjiu Dai
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: energy balance model, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, Southern Ocean, millennial-scale, CMIP, climate feedback, CO2, ensemble
Abstract Surface warming patterns modulate climate feedbacks. Ocean heat exchange redistributes heat between the upper and deep ocean, shaping warming patterns. However, its influence on climate feedbacks remains unclear. We explore this issue in the CMIP6 abrupt-4×CO2 experiment by dividing the simulation into fast, intermediate and slow phases and using an effective upper–deep ocean heat exchange coefficient (γ) inferred from a two-layer energy balance model. The intermediate phase stands out as the period when ocean heat exchange leaves its strongest imprint on warming patterns and climate feedbacks. Models with stronger ocean heat exchange (high-γ ensemble) differ from those with weaker exchange (low-γ ensemble) in both background ocean state and response, exhibiting weaker mean-state stratification and a stronger Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) favoring stronger heat penetration, subsurface warming, and distinct warming pattern and feedback evolution. Across the three phases, the low-γ ensemble sustains intensified warming in the tropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean alongside subdued warming in the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. However, the high-γ ensemble experiences a warming pattern reversal over these regions, tied to stronger intermediate-phase heat penetration and AMOC weakening. This centennial-scale warming pattern reversal, overlooked in previous work, partly mirrors the millennial-scale reversal previously found in multi-millennial abrupt-4×CO2 simulations. The high-γ ensemble also exhibits a larger increase and later peak change in net climate feedback. These findings highlight ocean heat exchange and associated ocean mean-state differences as key controls on time-evolving warming patterns and climate feedbacks.

item.title: Late Quaternary lake filling and drying in northern Australia's largest freshwater lake
item.dc:creator: Tim J. Cohen, Zenobia L. Jacobs, Caitlyn Scobie, Samuel K. Marx, William Reynolds, MATTHEW S. FORBES, … (+9)
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: marine isotope stage, MIS stage, Holocene, Quaternary, Bayesian
ABSTRACT Lake Woods, Jurrkulu, is northern Australia's largest freshwater lake filled today in strong Indo–Australian summer monsoons (IASM) to maximum depths of ~5 m. On the western margins of the lake, two large arcuate ridges occur 20 to 40 m above the lake floor and inset within these are other mid‐elevation lake deposits, such as depositional ridges, which suggest past filling events much higher than the modern maximum. We have undertaken the analysis of 20 samples for single‐grain optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) from shoreline and lake‐floor deposits and supplemented this chronology with an analysis of the basin hypsometry, basin‐wide erosion rates and rare earth elements to ascertain the dominant source of the large source‐bordering ridges. The outer and inner arcuate ridges represent both aeolian accumulation and inferred lake‐level highstands due to the presence of fine gravel facies and gastropods contained within them. We document two lake highstands at 195 ± 16 ka and at 98 ± 7 ka (20 and 15 m above the lake floor, respectively; the lake floor is 197 m Australian Height Datum, AHD). We also present a third but undated filling event 18.5 m above the lake floor (215.5 m AHD) but that is bracketed by two OSL ages of 91 ± 5 and 52 ± 3 ka, with a Bayesian modelled boundary age for lake filling of 95.9 to 53.8 ka (95% credible interval; C.I.). We find no evidence of the previously reported late Marine Isotope Stage [MIS] 3 highstand deposits and the prevalence of gully‐filled structureless sediments, dated to the mid to late Holocene, many of which contain archaeological artefacts that do not allow for the quantification of any accurate Holocene lake‐filling episodes. The lake floor is characterised by deeply cracking silts and clays, with single‐grain OSL results supporting significant post‐depositional mixing (maximum ages are <143 ka). Denudation rate data from detrital stream sediment samples indicate some of the lowest rates of denudation in northern Australia, of between 2.05 ± 0.51 and 0.83 ± 0.23 m/Myr, with the latter rate stemming from the dominant catchment area in the Barkly Tablelands. Sediment provenance data indicate that the slowly eroding Barkly Tablelands is the dominant source for the clays and silts in the lake basin. Despite being the largest lake in northern Australia, the slow rates of catchment‐wide erosion coupled with the intermittent filling have only produced a discontinuous record of the IASM, but one that shows exceptional episodic filling in MIS 5 to 4.

item.title: Late-glacial and Holocene vegetation dynamics in response to climate, land use and fire at Lago di Andromia (Ossola, Italian Alps)
item.dc:creator: Lionel de Montmollin, Lieveke van Vugt, Christoph Schwörer, Erika Gobet, Sina C. Aregger, Valentine Paquet, … (+6)
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: Holocene, proxy, sediment core
Understanding of past vegetation dynamics provides valuable information to better assess future ecosystem impacts under global change. In this context, the European Alps offer the opportunity to study diverse environments. Here, we present a multi-proxy palaeoecological study from the Pennine Alps combining pollen, spores, stomata, charcoal and plant macrofossil analysis. We reconstructed the vegetation dynamics over the past ca. 14,000 years based on sediment cores from Lago di Andromia (1926 m a.s.l.), a small lake located in the subalpine belt of the Ossola valley (Italy). During the Allerød the site was just above the treeline, before Larix decidua trees reached it ca. 11,500 years ago, in response to Holocene warming. Pinus cembra established locally ca. 500 years later, whereas Abies alba reached the site at the latest ca. 10,500 years ago and became co-dominant after 10,000 cal yr BP . Our new evidence confirms that the Ossola valley was an important corridor for the spread of Abies alba across the Alps, highlighting the crucial role of mid-to high elevations for its Holocene range expansion. Vegetation structure and composition remained rather stable during the Holocene Thermal Maximum (ca. 10,000–5000 cal yr BP). Earliest evidence for local pastoralism dates to 5500 years ago and was linked to anthropogenic fires to clear forests. During the Early Bronze Age (ca. 4200 years ago), both pastoral and arable farming increased in the valley, leading to a marked opening in the vegetation. Although sparse, evidence of Juglans regia cultivation during the Late-Neolithic coincides with similar results in Northern Italy, suggesting a striking centrality of the Andromia area, likely tied to its position at the confluence of five Alpine valleys close to the present-day city of Domodossola.

item.title: Using a two-stage Rosenbrock solver to increase computational efficiency in the DOE's Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1)
item.dc:creator: Rong-You Chien, Joshua S. Fu
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system, solver
We implemented a two-stage Rosenbrock solver (ROS2) in E3SMv1 and evaluated it with two atmospheric chemistry mechanisms. At a 180 s timestep, ROS2 reduced chemistry integration time by ~33% versus the original implicit solver on Cori/KNL CPUs, while maintaining stable one-year simulations and small ozone differences (≤1.03 ppb). Species-dependent differences in ozone, NO, NO2, and OH were small. Results support ROS2 as a lower-cost option, with further convergence and CPU/GPU testing needed.

item.title: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale baroclinic instabilities with MPAS-O (vE3SM3.0.0) – Part 1: Idealized experiments
item.dc:creator: Kyle E. Hinson, Dylan R. Schlichting, Robert D. Hetland, Darren Engwirda, Katherine M. Smith, Mark R. Petersen, … (+1)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Physical dynamics of ocean flows at fine spatial scales are challenging for regional and global scale ocean models due to high computational effort associated with smaller grid cell sizes. We compared two ocean models: a regional model (ROMS; Regional Ocean Modeling System) and global model (MPAS-O; Model for Prediction Across Scales – Ocean) across a range of resolutions (10 km to 100 m) in an idealized domain, and found that their similarities may hold promise for future coupling between them.
